Q: OpenSAML Signing with Azure Key Vault using Azure's KeyVaultJcaProvider : engineInitSign() not supported A:

Solution 1: Ensure you're getting KeyVaultPrivateKey

When using Azure KeyVault KeyStore, the key should already be a KeyVaultPrivateKey:

KeyStore keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("AzureKeyVault");

KeyVaultLoadStoreParameter param = new KeyVaultLoadStoreParameter(

System.getProperty("azure.keyvault.uri"));

keyStore.load(param);

PrivateKey privateKey = (PrivateKey) keyStore.getKey(alias, "".toCharArray());

// Verify it's the correct type

System.out.println("Key type: " + privateKey.getClass().getName());

// Should print: com.azure.security.keyvault.jca.KeyVaultPrivateKey

If your key is not a KeyVaultPrivateKey, you may be loading from the wrong keystore.

Solution 2: Control Provider Priority

Place the Sun RSA provider ahead of KeyVault for signature operations:

// Remove and re-add SunRsaSign at position 1

Provider sunProvider = Security.getProvider("SunRsaSign");

if (sunProvider != null) {

Security.removeProvider("SunRsaSign");

Security.insertProviderAt(sunProvider, 1);

}

// Add KeyVault provider after SunRsaSign

Security.insertProviderAt(new KeyVaultJcaProvider(), 2);

This ensures standard RSA signatures use Sun's implementation while KeyVault handles key storage.

Solution 3: Use Azure SDK Directly

Bypass JCA entirely and use Azure Key Vault Cryptography client for signing:

CryptographyClient cryptoClient = new CryptographyClientBuilder()

.keyIdentifier("https://<vault>.vault.azure.net/keys/<key-name>")

.credential(new DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder().build())

.buildClient();

// Sign a digest

SignResult result = cryptoClient.sign(SignatureAlgorithm.RS256, digestBytes);

byte[] signature = result.getSignature();

You'll need to implement a custom OpenSAML SignerProvider to integrate this approach.

Solution 4: Specify Provider Explicitly

For manual signing operations, specify the provider explicitly:

Provider sunProvider = Security.getProvider("SunRsaSign");

Signature sig = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA", sunProvider);

sig.initSign(privateKey);

sig.update(dataToSign);

byte[] signature = sig.sign();

Q: Pickling error work-around when passing decorators to multiprocessing module A:

Thanks to @Sébastien Guarnay for the great solution to my question. Using partial may be the perfect way to create "parameterized" functions. In reading up on partial, I also learned of a new feature in Python 3.14 - the functools.Placeholder. This allows for flexibility in where to place the fixed "parameters" vs. variables, e.g.

import functools

def f_trig(x,m):
    return cos(x*m)

_x = Placeholder
f = functools.partial(f_trig,_x,m)

Other advantages of partial , and the new Placeholder feature.

  • Almost twice as fast as alternatives (see below). For example, partial is faster than using a class with a defined __call__ function.

  • functions created using partial can be passed to multiprocessing processes without any pickling errors. In fact, partial functions can be created locally, and still avoid pickling errors.

  • partial Requires less code than alternatives (class, decorator).

  • The Placeholder allows for more natural arrangement of arguments in many cases, and doesn't produce any cost overhead. This is especially convenient for legacy code in which arguments cannot be easily re-ordered.

  • When using mathematical solvers that require a function (e.g. ODE solvers, integration routines), partial along with Placeholder offers an alternative to passing function parameters using an optional *args argument.

See some examples below

from dataclasses import dataclass
from functools import partial, Placeholder, wraps

from math import cos

def f_trig(x,m):
    return cos(m*x)

def fwrap(f,qname,*args):
    @wraps(f)
    def wrapper(x):
        return f(x,*args)
    wrapper.__qualname__ = qname
    return wrapper

@dataclass
class c_trig:
    m : int
    def __call__(self,x):
        return f_trig(x,self.m)

# "Decorator"
f1 = fwrap(f_trig,'f1',m:=2)

# Class
f2 = c_trig(m)

# from functools
_x = Placeholder
f3 = partial(f_trig,_x,m)


print(f1(2))
print(f2(2))
print(f3(2))
print("")

print("Using original decorator idea")
%timeit f1(2)
print("")

print("Using dataclass object")
%timeit f2(2)
print("")

print("Using partial")
%timeit f3(2)
print("")

Timing results :

-0.6536436208636119
-0.6536436208636119
-0.6536436208636119

Using original decorator idea
163 ns ± 1.08 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000,000 loops each)

Using dataclass object
131 ns ± 0.61 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000,000 loops each)

Using partial
92.1 ns ± 0.574 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000,000 loops each)

partial is about 1.8x speed-up over my original decorator idea and about 1.4x speed-up over using a callable class object.

Q: Use named parameters when calling a Powershell class method A:

It is hard to imaging how you jump from functions that suffer from a performance overhead to a class with a static method (as apposed to an instance created from a class with a <convertable-value-type> syntax).

PowerShell might indeed have some performance issues with regards to function calls (see also #19322) but there are a lot of ways to define and invoke a function, see: What is the best way to reuse static code.

Fyi, from my benchmarks, it appears that the foreach method might be even faster than using a class:

$MyMethod = { Write-Host $_.a $_.b }
@{ a = 1; b = 2 }.foreach($MyMethod)

Saying that, it might be a good idea to share an example of the original "thousands of calls of a function" knowing that there are several PowerShell pitfalls where it concerns performance (along with a general PowerShell Pipeline misconception) and where it is still recommended to use the (correct) idiomatic PowerShell syntax for better "readability" (quote from PowerShell scripting performance considerations):

ℹ️ Note

Many of the techniques described here aren't idiomatic PowerShell and may reduce the readability of a PowerShell script. Script authors are advised to use idiomatic PowerShell unless performance dictates otherwise.

Q: Twilio Conversations Group MMS not working A:

I have not seen any additional press release, so this is likely your issue. Twilio had issues at the carrier level and blocked groupmms for all new customers. So if you have an older account (or access to one) you can potentially use it, but otherwise as of their last statement you can't use it at the moment still.

The work around I've seen is to use conversations and distributed it a message via a one to many channel, but I have not tried this myself and I'm not familiar with the drawback.

Also there are limitations on the phone numbers as well.
